params.text:
The duty to make complaining easy

The regulations require every service to have a complaints procedure that is clear, published and genuinely accessible. CQC Regulation 16 expects providers to operate an effective system for identifying, receiving, recording, handling and responding to complaints. It is not enough to have a policy in a folder — people must actually know how to complain and feel able to.

  • Tell people how to complain, who to, and what will happen next.
  • Provide information in formats and languages people can understand — easy read, large print, translated, or spoken.
  • Give people time, and help them put their concerns into words if they find that hard.
  • Make sure no one fears that complaining will affect the care they receive.

A barrier-free culture

Accessibility is about attitude as much as paperwork. The people you support are often in a vulnerable position, and many worry that if they complain their care will suffer, or that staff will treat them differently. This fear of reprisal is one of the biggest reasons complaints go unspoken. Part of your job is to make clear, in words and in how you behave, that raising a concern is welcomed and will never be held against them. When people trust that, they tell us about problems while they are still small.

Advocacy and communication needs

Complaining should be genuinely possible for everyone, not just those who are confident and articulate. Some people will need extra support to be heard, and you should know where to turn.

  • Independent advocacy: anyone can ask for an independent advocate, and offering access to advocacy is part of an accessible procedure. NHS Complaints Advocacy is free and available to help people make a complaint about health or social care.
  • Communication needs: use easy-read leaflets, pictures, interpreters, or communication aids so the person’s own voice comes through.
  • People who know them: with the person’s agreement, family or friends can help express a concern that is hard to put into words.

Never assume someone has no complaint simply because they cannot easily tell you one.

params.alt: A care worker sitting with an older person they support, beside the heading “The duty to make complaining easy”. Key points: Independent advocacy; Communication needs; People who know them.

params.question: Which of these help make a complaints procedure genuinely accessible?

answers.text: Offering the information in easy read, large print and other languages.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Information must be available in formats and languages that meet people’s needs.

answers.text: Providing an advocate for someone who would find it hard to complain alone.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Support to complain, including advocacy, is part of an accessible system.

answers.text: Only accepting complaints if they are put in a formal letter.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Insisting on one rigid format is a barrier; complaints can be made in many ways.

answers.text: Reassuring people that complaining will never affect their care.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Removing fear of reprisal is essential to a truly accessible culture.

params.textField: No one should fear *reprisal* for raising a concern about their care. Where a person struggles to put a complaint into words, an independent *advocate* can speak up on their behalf. Information should be offered in accessible formats such as *easy-read* so everyone can understand it. For someone who does not speak English, an *interpreter* helps them to be heard. Never assume a person who cannot easily speak has no *concern* worth listening to.
